item.title: Educational Psychology Improves Use of AI for Learning
item.description:
Education

Educational Psychology Improves Use of AI for Learning

Students can work with AI to support their motivation and engagement.

Posted July 8, 2026

Key points
  • AI works best when it supports thinking, not when it replaces student learning.
  • Educational psychology helps students use AI to build motivation and engagement.
  • AI prompts can strengthen planning, persistence, confidence, and learning focus.
  • AI should coach students toward learning, not complete their work.

Post by Andrew J. Martin, PhD

How Is Generative AI Being Used?

Used well, AI has significant potential to support learners’ academic development. Yet despite its promise, students often use AI inefficiently. Many rely on AI primarily to complete tasks rather than deepen their learning, often outsourcing too much of their thinking in the process. In classrooms, the use of generative AI is frequently ad hoc, with students experimenting through trial and error, with teachers providing inconsistent guidance. At the same time, schools and universities lack coherent frameworks for what productive AI-supported learning should actually look like.

The upshot is that the most advanced educational technology in history is too frequently being used with very little psychological guidance.

Teaching Students How to Learn with Generative AI

Generative AI works best when students approach it as an active learning partner rather than a passive answer machine. For example, a student overwhelmed by an upcoming exam might use AI not to generate answers, but to break revision into manageable steps, reduce anxiety about falling behind, or build confidence through small achievable goals.

This requires a significant shift in educational thinking. Poor approach: “How can AI do this task for the student?” Better approach: “How can AI help the student become a more capable learner?”

When students develop the capacity to partner with AI productively, AI can become a powerful learning support.

Educational Psychology Can Inform Productive AI Learning Partnerships

Educational psychology has spent decades identifying specific processes and factors that support effective learning. Educational psychology can help students use AI in ways that target specific, evidence-based aspects of learning.

Student motivation and engagement are a case in point. AI prompting informed by educational psychology supports learners in developing specific and structured prompts aimed at, for example, building self-belief, strengthening persistence, enhancing planning, and reducing anxiety.

This prompting is vital because different learners face distinct psychological barriers. A student with low self-belief requires different support from a student with poor planning.

The Motivation and Engagement Wheel

The wheel's framework unpacks these specific factors. The wheel (Figure 1) comprises 11 specific factors grouped in four broad domains: positive and negative motivation, and engagement.

Figure 1. The Motivation and Engagement Wheel
Source: Reproduced with permission from Lifelong Achievement Group.

Positive motivation and engagement include the thoughts, feelings, and behaviors that help students to learn effectively:

  • Self-belief: Confidence in one’s ability to succeed in learning tasks.
  • Valuing: Seeing learning as useful, meaningful, or important.
  • Learning focus: Focusing on understanding, improvement, and skill development.
  • Planning: Organizing and monitoring study and academic tasks.
  • Task management: Managing time, distractions, and study routines effectively.
  • Persistence: Continuing to work through challenges and difficulties.

Negative motivation and engagement comprise factors that can interfere with students’ learning:

  • Anxiety: Worry or nervousness about academic tasks or performance.
  • Failure avoidance: Focusing on avoiding poor performance or disappointment.
  • Uncertain control: Feeling unsure about how to succeed academically.
  • Self-sabotage: Behaviors that undermine success, such as procrastination or avoidance.
  • Disengagement: Withdrawal from learning through reduced effort or involvement.

The GenAI Motivation and Learning Buddy

The learning buddy is an open-access tool that draws on the above wheel to support students’ learning. There are 11 GenAI Buddy prompt scripts—one for each of the 11 parts of the wheel.

The GenAI buddy functions as an AI-supported coach. Rather than providing answers, it helps learners maintain motivation and engagement as they complete academic tasks such as preparing for an examination, completing homework, writing an essay, or studying for a presentation.

For example, instead of asking AI to “write my essay introduction,” the student copies a buddy prompt script into an AI tool and is guided through strategies to help reduce anxiety before starting the introduction, strengthen confidence about planning the structure, or improve persistence during revision.

In this sense, the AI becomes less of a content generator and more of a support for motivation.

The buddy is carefully structured to keep students actively engaged in learning rather than passively consuming answers. It includes key elements that transform the AI interaction from passive content consumption into an active process of guided motivation and engagement. For example, each prompt script includes:

  • A working definition of the specific part of the wheel the student has selected to focus on
  • A clearly defined role that establishes the AI as a learning coach rather than a task-completer
  • Explicit rules and guardrails that reinforce academic integrity, student agency, and responsible AI use
  • Format requirements so outputs are organized, accessible, and manageable for diverse learners
  • Relevant educational psychology theory to ensure the AI’s responses are psychologically informed
  • Evidence-based motivation and engagement strategies for students to select from
  • Self-complete exercises for students to apply their selected strategy
  • Structured reflection that promotes metacognition and self-awareness
  • Encouragement in the event students encounter setbacks or roadblocks

The Educational Challenge Ahead

Learners need guidance on how to use AI effectively, and educational psychology provides principles and practices to support this.

As AI becomes more capable, the role of educational psychology becomes increasingly important to help students use it in ways that preserve their agency as learners and support meaningful learning.

The author, Andrew J. Martin, Ph.D., is a professor of educational psychology at UNSW Australia and a Fellow of APA’s Division 15. His areas of interest are student motivation, engagement, learning, and quantitative research methods.

item.title: AI and the First Principles of Thought
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

AI and the First Principles of Thought

Human cognition may finally have a counterpart evolution didn't build.

Posted July 8, 2026

Key points
  • Anthropic found a workspace inside Claude where thoughts form before any words appear.
  • It raises questions about human cognition we could never ask before.
  • A window into AI may show us the first principles of cognition.
Source: Sebastian / Pixabay

Recently, I posted something about AI that I didn’t expect to write for years, if ever. I admitted that the interior of these systems may not be the empty room I’ve long described. Anthropic has identified what it calls the J-space, a small set of internal patterns that behave like a mental workspace. Concepts take shape there and influence answers without ever appearing in the final text. The researchers can watch a thought form inside the machine before it speaks. I haven’t stopped thinking about that.

Two details stand out to me. First, no one engineered this workspace. It emerged on its own during training. Second, when researchers suppressed the J-space, basic recall survived, but complex reasoning collapsed. Whatever the structure is, it isn’t decoration. And when you remove it, the thinking stops.

Let’s start here. Studying cognition meant studying ourselves. Every capable mind we could examine came from evolution, including the one doing the examining. AI breaks that monopoly. Whatever else these systems are, they’re a second implementation of advanced cognition, reached by a completely different route. And this “second implementation” lets us ask something that used to be unaskable: Does thinking have first principles?

One possibility, I believe, is yes. Cognition, like vision or flight, may have only a few workable engineering solutions. Evolution found a workspace in us. Training found one in the machine. Octopus eyes and human eyes converged on nearly the same optics through lineages that split more than five hundred million years ago, and nobody calls the octopus a copy.

This perspective has serious backing. Stanislas Dehaene and Lionel Naccache, two of the architects of global workspace theory in human consciousness, reviewed the Anthropic work and provided this striking perspective.

The global workspace may provide a universal computational solution to the problem of flexible processing, one that biological and artificial systems converge on when they must chain reasoning, reuse intermediate results, and report on their own processing.

If they’re right, we’ve glimpsed a principle of thought itself.

The other possibility is stranger. Every word the model learned came from minds that already work this way. Maybe the machine built its workspace by copying the one thing all its training data had in common—us. In that case, we haven’t found a principle of cognition. We’ve found our own reflection, buried deeper in the machine than anyone expected.

What saves this from being a hypothetical construct is that it can be tested. Train a system mostly on non-human data like protein folding or weather and watch if a similar workspace appears. If it does, that would point to a law. If it doesn’t, the workspace starts to look like something we handed the machine without meaning to. The researchers themselves list this as an open question. So, the experiment is sitting there, waiting to be put to the test.

Either answer changes what we know. One says thinking has first principles, and we can finally go looking. The other says the most convincing mind we ever built is a copy of the only one we had to copy, and we’d never tell the difference from inside our own heads.

I’ve spent three years arguing that these machines think with no mind behind the thinking. This is the first finding that could prove me wrong. It could also be the best evidence that I was right. I don’t know which.

item.title: Sometimes Your Child Isn't Triggering You: Your Childhood Is
item.description:
Parenting

Sometimes Your Child Isn't Triggering You: Your Childhood Is

Why ordinary parenting moments can awaken old wounds for parents with ADHD

Posted July 8, 2026

Key points
  • Parenting can trigger unresolved childhood wounds, not just reactions to our child’s behavior in the moment.
  • Parents, especially those with ADHD, may misinterpret ordinary defiance as personal failure due to past shame.
  • Healing happens when parents become aware of old patterns and intentionally choose new responses.

Have you ever found yourself reacting to your child in a way that surprised you?

Your daughter refuses to get dressed for school, and you find yourself feeling overwhelmed and defeated. Your son rolls his eyes when you ask him to put away his phone, and it leaves you questioning whether he respects you at all. Or perhaps your child melts down over something seemingly minor, and although the situation was resolved within minutes, you carry the emotional weight of it for the rest of the day.

Source: Karola G/Pexels

Every parent has moments like these. Parenting is demanding, unpredictable, and emotionally taxing. For parents with ADHD, however, the challenges can feel even greater. Staying organized while managing a household, tolerating constant interruptions, regulating your own emotions while helping your child regulate theirs, and navigating the sensory demands of family life can leave even the most loving ADHD parent exhausted and depleted.

Yet over the years, both in my clinical practice and in my research, I have started thinking differently about these moments. Sometimes the intensity of our emotional reactions has surprisingly little to do with what our child has just done. Rather, it reflects the meaning our brain has attached to that behavior.

I was reminded of this recently while interviewing ADHD coach and father of two, Clay Gill. We talked about executive functioning, emotional regulation, and the everyday realities of raising children when your own brain works differently. As the interview unfolded, I noticed that we kept returning to his childhood (I find many parenting stories lead here).

Clay described becoming a father as one of the experiences that finally brought his ADHD “front and center.” Like many adults who are diagnosed later in life, Clay had spent years honing ways to compensate for his difficulties, but parenthood changed that. Under the relentless cognitive and emotional demands of raising children, Clay’s strategies for compensating and holding things together began to give way.

As we talked, however, I realized that Clay wasn’t only describing the challenges of parenting with ADHD; he was describing moments when ordinary interactions with his children raised long-standing feelings of shame and inadequacy to the surface.

Clay described many common parenting scenarios, for example, hearing the word “no” from his child (not an unusual situation for the parent of a toddler, certainly). Yet Clay realized that his emotional reactions often felt much larger than the situations themselves.

Source: Esra Korkmaz/Pexels

As psychologists, we often remind parents that children’s behavior is communication. I think there is another side to this, though; sometimes our reactions are communicating something as well. In fact, they may be telling us less about the child standing in front of us and more about the experiences we carry from our own childhood.

Like most parents with young children, Clay finds it challenging when one of his children refuses a request. Perhaps they don’t want to put on their shoes or stop playing when it’s time to leave. We’ve all had moments like these. What caught Clay’s attention was not his child’s behavior, but the intensity of his own emotional response. As an insightful person and an ADHD coach, Clay began asking himself why.

Clay realized that hearing the word “no” wasn’t simply frustrating. It seemed to touch something much older within him. He had grown up with the belief that children should respect and obey their parents. When his own children resisted, his brain wasn’t interpreting it as typical childhood behavior. Instead, it felt personal, as though their refusal reflected something fundamental about him as a father.

Our brains are constantly interpreting the world around us. We don’t simply respond to events; we respond to what we believe those events mean. One parent hears “no” and thinks, “My child is having a hard day.” Another hears “no” and immediately thinks, “My child doesn’t respect me.” The behavior is identical; the interpretation is not.

Source: Mart Productions / Pexels

As Clay continued reflecting on his experiences, he told me about getting his family out the door that morning. As the minutes passed and his children weren’t ready, Clay’s thoughts quickly shifted toward disappointing other people. He imagined arriving late, being judged, and confirming that he was unreliable. What distressed him most was not the clock on the wall or even his children’s behavior, but what being late might say about him.

Many adults with ADHD have accumulated years of experiences that shape how they see themselves and have a loud inner critic. Some remember report cards filled with comments about not paying attention or not working hard enough. Others recall being called lazy, careless, emotional, dramatic, or “too much.” Those experiences do not disappear simply because we become adults or parents. Unconsciously, they become the lens through which we interpret everyday parenting experiences.

When I listened to Clay describe these moments, I found myself thinking that perhaps the most difficult parenting situations are not always the loudest or most dramatic ones. Sometimes they are the ordinary moments that awaken familiar beliefs we have carried for decades without realizing they are still there.

As our conversation continued, Clay shared a memory from his childhood that helped him make sense of many of these parenting experiences.

Source: Helena Lopes / Pexels

He described himself as a “bedroom kid.”

If family life was calm and everyone was getting along, little Clay was welcome to be with his parents. But if he became loud, emotional, or disruptive, the message was that it was time to leave. He remembers spending much of his childhood in his bedroom or outside entertaining himself. Looking back, though, Clay does not describe his parents as uncaring. Rather, he recognizes that they were doing the best they could with the knowledge and resources they had at the time.

Today, he and his wife have made a conscious decision to create something different for their own children.

“I want living room kids,” he told me.

Clay wants his children to know that they belong with the family, even when they are loud, emotional, disappointed, or difficult. They do not have to earn his closeness by being easy to parent.

I found myself thinking about many of the parents I have worked with over the years. We often imagine that parenting is about teaching children how to navigate the world. And of course it is. But parenting also has a way of reconnecting us with experiences we have not thought about in years.

Source: Gustavo Fring / Pexels

Sometimes those memories are joyful. Sometimes they’re painful. More often, they are subtle enough that we have never fully appreciated just how much they continue to influence us.

Parents occasionally tell me, “I don’t want my children to experience what I experienced growing up.” My conversation with Clay made it clear that this intention often appears in very ordinary moments. It appears when a parent simply sits beside a child during a meltdown. It appears in the father who apologizes after losing his temper because apologies were rare in his own home. It appears in the mother who makes space for her child’s big emotions after spending years believing that her own feelings were too much for other people.

These decisions are rarely made consciously in the moment. They often evolve from experiences that have become part of how we understand relationships, safety, and belonging.

Source: Timur Weber / Pexels

One of the things I appreciated most about Clay’s reflections was his willingness to revisit those early experiences without becoming trapped by them. He did not describe his childhood as an excuse for his parenting struggles, nor did he speak about his parents with resentment. Instead, he seemed interested in understanding the connections between the child he once was and the father he is trying to become.

I have found that many parents become gentler with themselves once they recognize that not every emotional reaction begins in the present. Sometimes a child’s behavior touches experiences that were never fully understood or named. Bringing those experiences into awareness does not erase them, but it can soften their hold.

Toward the end of my conversation with Clay, I found myself thinking less about ADHD and more about healing during parenthood. Clay’s children have given him opportunities, almost every day, to notice an old pattern and choose a different response.

Parenting can do that; it has a way of showing us parts of ourselves we thought we had left behind. Understanding those patterns does not change our childhood. It may, however, change what happens next.

item.title: What Will Banning Transgirls From Sports Mean for Other Girls?
item.description:
Transgender

What Will Banning Transgirls From Sports Mean for Other Girls?

Personal Perspective: An analysis of West Virginia v. B.P.J. and Little v. Hecox.

Posted July 8, 2026

Key points
  • A new Supreme Court decision allows states to unilaterally ban transgender girls from girls teams.
  • The ruling may have effects on all girls, not just transgender girls.
  • Any young woman could be accused of not being a "real" girl and face consequences.
US Supreme Court
Source: Malcolm Hill / Pexels

The most recent Supreme Court ruling about transgender girls in sports is no doubt a major blow to transgender athletes, although as Carrie Costello wrote in their blog, it is not anywhere as bad as it could be. It was not a broad ruling denying transgender rights; it was a narrow ruling indicating something was distinctive about sports, and so the ruling only applied narrowly to school sports. Still, this is one more decision dismissing the needs and rights of gender-nonconforming youngsters. And I encourage you to read about those effects.

In this column, however, I’m inspired by thoughts recently tweeted by sociologist Jessie Calarco on BlueSky:

As the mom of a cisgender girl athlete, I’m worried not only about the potential invasion of privacy (and bodily autonomy) but about the pressure that the threat of gender inspection could put on girl athletes (cis and trans) to present themselves in stereotypically gendered ways.

I share this concern. The new threat of being identified as not a “real” girl depends on how people “read” your body, how you dress, how you move, and the confidence with which you speak. Any girl not deemed feminine enough for her school principal, or the parents of her teammates, can be challenged as not being a “real” girl and then investigated. The court provided few guidelines for the implementation of its ruling. How does a school district know if a child transitioned before ever enrolling? How does a school know if a transfer student was assigned a different sex at birth from the gender they present as an adolescent? Imagine the characteristics of a girl accused of not being a girl at all.

I think it is instructive to think about the girls who were accused of witchcraft in Salem. They were often nonconformists who danced in the woods, or women who used herbs to heal the sick. But accusations went beyond being atypical; accusations were also made against one's enemies. And accusation alone creates stigma and distrust. I worry about what happens now to girls who flaunt what sociologists call emphasized femininity, an obsession with appearing attractive to boys and always being polite and subordinate. Will falling in line with stereotypical feminine traits become the only way to rise above suspicion of not belonging on a girls' team? Will girls who prefer to wear baggy pants and T-shirts, or prefer not to shave their legs, be among those accused? Will young butch lesbians be targeted? Unfortunately, the only way to protect oneself from an accusation may be to adopt a conservative version of feminine subordination, at least when not on the playing field. This decision and its implementation therefore risk inhibiting the freedom of all girls, cisgender and transgender, by creating a system that allows accusations against anyone who does not seem feminine enough.

For decades, feminists have been arguing that emphasized femininity is oppressive, that girls should be free to dress comfortably and ignore the social requirement to diet, paint their face, and wear high heels. But it is possible that only those who perform their femininity most traditionally will be free from accusations of not being a “real” girl. What happens then to those girls accused? How does an 8-year-old prove she has female genitalia and XX chromosomes? Shall we subject them to invasive vaginal inspection long before they are old enough for the gynecologist's office? Shall we require them to have chromosome tests? Or, perhaps, to avoid such discrimination against gender-nonconforming girls, every young female athlete will need to have their chromosomes tested, or their vaginas inspected. And who will pay for all this testing? And how do the girls deal with the invasion of their privacy? Will we test every child to find one that doesn’t belong? We must face the potentially Draconian impact of this decision on every American girl who participates in school sports. They may now feel as if the safest thing to do to protect their dignity and avoid accusations is to act as traditionally feminine as possible. Their parents and coaches may dislike this but realize it’s better than having their daughters or athletes charged with not being a real girl and having their bodily privacy invaded. Will we push lesbian athletes back into the closet to avoid discrimination?

You may ask, what about transgender girls who have gone through puberty and have significant advantages over cisgender girls? Isn’t that unfair? It may be, but that depends on so many other factors: whether the child has been on puberty blockers since before their teen years, whether their sport requires specific skills that are sex-differentiated, and the age of the athletes involved. Every district can have policies that can be enforced on a case-by-case basis but the Constitution does not allow us to discriminate against an entire group to protect another. We must carefully weigh the context of each case and try to find the most equitable solution. Congress needs to act to protect all girls so that they are free to be feminine or masculine, warm and nurturant, or bold and bossy. By excluding transgender girls, we may end up requiring all girls to stay in a conservative lane. This Supreme Court decision is one more that takes America back to an earlier, misogynistic time before the second wave of feminism. May some future Congress legislate the right for us all to be fully human and not restricted to the straitjackets of traditional femininity or masculinity. I’m hopeful but not holding my breath.

item.title: How Time Shapes Our Lives and the Fiction of Memory
item.description:
Memory

How Time Shapes Our Lives and the Fiction of Memory

Exploring time perception and memory through fiction.

Posted July 8, 2026

The clock on the wall may tick away while the calendar marks the passage of days, but our psychological experience of time does not necessarily mirror the tools we use to measure it. As author Shea Ernshaw suggests, "Time is a slippery thing."

Ernshaw’s latest novel, Habits of the Sea, explores time perception and memory, and how unforgettable people and places pull us to redefine home.

Time can be understood as a mental construct of our reality, helping us to organize our life’s experiences. While our daily lives unfold continuously, when we reflect on the past we tend to remember experiences as distinct and cohesive events, like chapters in a novel (Clewett et al., 2019).

An external sense of place and our internal emotional experiences both play a critical role in shaping our memories (Cohn-Sheehy & Ranganath, 2017). When we recall events from our past, we might "see" ourselves in that place, with all of the emotions contained in that moment flooding us once again.

For Ernshaw, bending the rules of time in Habits of the Sea offered an opportunity to explore what happens when we courageously step into the unfamiliar.

Q: Share a bit about your background and what inspired you to write Habits of the Sea.

Shea Ernshaw: My ancestors were part of the Watson clan from Cellardyke, a small fishing village in the East Neuk of Fife, Scotland. In 1871 they crossed the Atlantic and settled in Canada, where much of my family still lives today. Growing up, my mother shared the stories told to her by her grandmother, Zetta Watson, and they have always lived in the background of my imagination. I wondered what it must have felt like to stand at the edge of the sea, in a country that was all they’d ever known, and leave it behind. Habits of the Sea grew from that question. A need to understand what my ancestors might have faced. It became a story about the pull of the sea, about lost love, and the courage it takes to chase a life that doesn’t yet exist.

Source: Simon & Schuster/Used with permission

Q: In your novel, Clay lives on an island floating off the coast of Nova Scotia where time doesn’t pass in the same way that it does for the story’s protagonist, Ellie. How do these differences in time perception impact the relationship the two characters forge?

Shea Ernshaw: Time is a slippery thing in this story. For Clay, the island becomes a place of suspended grief after the loss of his wife and children. Because time passes more slowly on the island, his grief is something he can’t seem to escape. But for Ellie, time is a thief. It takes her old life—the one she left behind on the mainland—and steals it from her, making it impossible for her to ever go back. Without giving away too much, time is mercurial and untrustworthy in this story. It becomes the very thing that binds Ellie and Clay together.

Q: Research shows that we tend to remember distinct events, despite the fact that our lives unfold continuously, and our memories are reconstructed from retrieved information that includes the environment and our internal state during the event. What role does the setting and emotions play in Clay and Ellie’s memories?

Shea Ernshaw: What a beautiful question. I’ve always been fascinated by how environments shape who we are and our memories. Sometimes a place can hold a version of ourselves that we’ve long ago left behind. Or even forgotten.

In Habits of the Sea, the island becomes like a vessel, holding all their emotions: grief, longing, hope. It’s a place that the main character, Ellie, can’t seem to forget even when she tries to move on in her life. And when she finally returns to the island, years later, it’s like stepping into a part of her memory she had convinced herself didn’t exist. I also think the isolation of the island allows the characters to fully excavate who they are, without interruption, without the outside world influencing how they should feel. It’s such a raw place to exist and live.

Q: In what way does Habits of the Sea explore the courage it takes to redefine home?

Shea Ernshaw: The idea of home has been a common theme in many of my books. I’m intrigued by our definition of home, how desperately we often to cling to it, and whether home is a place or if it’s something we can take with us.

Both Clay and Ellie are shaped by loss, and both of them are trying to understand where they belong in the world. I think the island represents one type of home—isolated and protected, but also frozen in time. For Ellie, she must risk leaving her old life behind, in exchange for the possibility of a new home on the island, and perhaps even uncover who she was always meant to be. She must cross an ocean—like my ancestors did—in the hope that something better awaits. It’s a risk many of us aren’t willing to take. I’m not sure I would.

But home isn’t always where we started. Sometimes it’s a thing we build along the way.

Q: Where do you most see yourself in this story? What did you learn about yourself in the process of writing it?

Shea Ernshaw: Writing this novel certainly made me to see how much of life is shaped by the choices we’re brave enough to make. The ones that frighten us. Uncertainty can be such a powerful way to transform your life. Right at the edge of what makes us uncomfortable, is sometimes where life truly begins. I can’t say that I’ve embraced this thesis fully since writing this novel. But I’m taking small steps across that line, testing the waters, before I dive right in.

Q: What do you hope readers take away from spending time with Habits of the Sea?

Shea Ernshaw: I hope readers feel like they were transported to Saltwell Island for a short while. I hope they feel the wind, the salt air, the wildness of the sea. But more than this, I also hope readers feel a sense of what might be waiting for them beyond the edges of their known world.

Perhaps what haunts us most, is the road we haven’t taken. The possibility of a life not yet lived. I hope we all stray a little from what feels familiar. There might be something wonderful waiting for us out there, off the edges of the map.

item.title: When a Child’s Disability or Mental Illness Hurts Siblings
item.description:
Family Dynamics

When a Child’s Disability or Mental Illness Hurts Siblings

Parenting tips to stop harmful sibling behaviors and meet each child’s needs.

Posted July 8, 2026

Key points
  • Children with disabilities or mental illnesses may behave aggressively and harm their siblings.
  • Parents may struggle to meet each child’s needs and provide a safe environment.
  • Practical tips can help reduce sibling harm, restore family calm, and instill healthy coping skills.
Source: Nuva Frames / Shutterstock

About 20 percent of children in the U.S. have been diagnosed with a mental, emotional, or behavioral disorder, and these conditions become more common as children age. Many of these children are part of families with multiple children, and parents are challenged to balance each child’s individual needs while supporting their sibling relationships.

In families with a child with a disability or mental health problems, siblings can share a positive relationship, even when the disability or disorder is severe. Warm sibling relationships are important for mental health across the lifespan and for a calm family atmosphere. Sometimes, however, sibling relationships are more challenging, and parents need help supporting their children and keeping them safe.

Hurt Siblings

Children with mental and behavioral disorders and intellectual disabilities can lash out or behave aggressively toward their siblings, sometimes resulting in harm. This may be due to quickly changing or lingering moods. Parents may see their child, when frustrated, reacting with anger to situations or people, leading to aggressive behavior. Children may also believe they are justified in resorting to harmful behavior to resolve disagreements.

Being on the receiving end of these behaviors, especially if they are chronic or unpredictable, can leave siblings feeling anxious and fearful. In some families, a sibling may be the sole target of their brother’s or sister’s aggression. For the harmed sibling, home may be a place of stress, and they may feel embarrassed and disturbed by their sibling’s behavior. Parents may also notice that the harmed sibling and other siblings in the family, particularly younger children, may start to act in the same aggressive ways as their sibling.

Parenting Siblings

In families in which one child has a disability or mental health problems, parents may struggle with supporting this child while stopping their harmful behavior towards their siblings. It is not unusual for parents to experience significant stress while balancing the needs of all their children, including their safety.

Parents may worry about the mental and physical health impact on their harmed children, especially if a sibling has traumatized them. This is a valid concern, as being harmed by a sibling is associated with children experiencing depression, trouble sleeping, and other negative impacts.

Children with disabilities or mental illnesses may have aggressive behaviors that are ongoing and intensify with age, resulting in parents feeling increasingly overwhelmed and hopeless. Prolonged parenting stress can reduce warm, effective parenting, and some parents may feel they have failed their children or are not good parents. Both mothers and fathers may feel this way, so parents need to take care of themselves and each other. This will help them be the parents they want to be for each child and have the time and energy to support healthy relationships between siblings.

Help for Parents and Their Children’s Sibling Relationships

Parents play a key role in their children’s sibling relationships. But it can be difficult for parents to know how to effectively help each of their children in this situation, especially when they have already tried several solutions. Parents may struggle to find relevant resources to help their children and relieve their own concerns. To help parents, children, and siblings, we provide several practical tips:

  1. Fostering a positive sibling relationship can begin in early childhood. Even in toddlerhood, parents can create opportunities for siblings to share activities they enjoy together. Be sure to praise any signs of positive and kind behavior among the children.
  2. Parents can reduce children’s aggressive behaviors (e.g., hitting, pushing) by teaching constructive ways to manage and resolve conflicts. There are free resources available to help parents guide their children’s behavior with their siblings (e.g., Play Nicely and SAARA).
  3. Hurt siblings may come to parents with their worries, and parents should be open to discussing their sibling’s harmful behaviors and taking action to protect the harmed child. These conversations can include teaching children about their sibling’s disorder or disability while promoting emotional and cognitive coping skills, such as calmly expressing themselves and problem-solving. It is important to assure children that they should always be treated with care and respect by others.
  4. Sibling relationships may be enhanced when children get a break from one another through one-on-one time with a parent and activities outside of the home, including with friends. Siblings can stay connected through shared family time, engaging in common interests, or daily activities.

Overall, it is important that parents monitor whether each child’s needs are being met and their sibling relationships are safe and healthy. If parents notice their child avoids their sibling, is unusually quiet, or has trouble sleeping, eating, engaging in their usual hobbies, getting along with friends, or managing schoolwork, outside help may be needed.

Parenting education and therapeutic help for each family member could improve communication and relationship dynamics. If these behavioral changes occur because a sibling’s behavior is severe or even abusive, children’s safety must be ensured. Pediatricians, family resource centers, and organizations like the National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI) can help with safety planning, resources, and referrals.

To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: What You Need for Career Success on Your Own Terms
item.description:
Career

What You Need for Career Success on Your Own Terms

Build a career that reflects your values, purpose, and well-being.

Posted July 8, 2026

Key points
  • Define career success based on your values, not outdated expectations or external pressure.
  • Sustainable career growth aligns ambition with well-being, purpose and your current season of life.
  • Confidence and strategic visibility help create opportunities before you feel completely ready.
  • Strong boundaries and the right support make long-term career success more achievable.
What You Need for Career Success on Your Own Terms
Source: Julia Amaral/AdobeStock

Most women inherit a definition of career success long before they consciously create one for themselves.

It often sounds something like this: work hard, keep progressing, say yes to opportunity, be grateful, stay visible enough to be considered, but not so visible that you seem self-promotional. Keep delivering, keep proving, keep moving.

For many women, this model works for a while. It can help you build capability, credibility, and experience. But at some point, it can also start to feel limiting.

You may be successful on paper, but tired in your body. You may be progressing, but not in a direction that feels meaningful. You may be respected, but not fully seen. You may be achieving but still wondering whether the version of success you’re chasing is actually yours.

That’s why career success on your own terms matters. It’s not about opting out of ambition. It’s about becoming more intentional with it. It’s about asking what success looks like when it reflects your values, your capacity, your leadership, your life, and the contribution you actually want to make.

Here are five things you need to begin creating career success on your own terms.

1. A clearer definition of success

The first step is to define what success means for you now. Not five years ago. Not according to your organization. Not according to your family, peers, industry, or younger self. Now, in this current season of your life and career.

Your definition of success may include progression, financial growth, influence, or leadership. It may also include flexibility, well-being, autonomy, meaning, or more time for life outside of work.

For many women, the challenge is that they keep pursuing goals they never really chose, or goals that made sense in an earlier season but no longer fit.

Ask yourself:

  • What does success look like for me in this season of my life and career?
  • What am I still chasing because I think I should?
  • What would I choose if I trusted my own priorities more?

You don’t need to have a perfect answer straight away. But you do need to begin the process of separating inherited success from intentional success.

2. A career direction that fits your life, not just your résumé

It’s easy to build a career based on the next logical step. A bigger role. A larger team. More responsibility. A higher title. There’s nothing wrong with any of those things if they’re aligned with your goals. But career growth that looks good externally can still feel wrong internally if it doesn’t fit the life you want to live.

This is why your career direction needs to be considered in the context of your whole life.

Ask yourself:

  • What kind of work energizes me now?
  • What kind of responsibility do I want to hold?
  • What kind of pace is sustainable for me?
  • What do I want my work to make possible in my life?

This is not about lowering your goals. It’s about making sure your ambition is pointing in the right direction.

You might decide that you do want the promotion, but with better boundaries. You might decide that you want to grow your influence without taking on a role that will consume your life. You might realize that your next step isn’t more, but different.

That clarity matters, and it’s worth spending time on.

3. The confidence to back yourself

Career success on your own terms requires confidence, but not the kind of confidence that’s loud, performative, or certain all the time. It requires the kind of confidence that helps you make decisions, speak up, advocate for yourself, and take action, even when you don’t feel completely ready.

Many women wait for confidence before they move. They wait until they feel more qualified, more certain, more prepared, more legitimate. But confidence often comes through action, not before it. If you’re waiting to feel completely ready, you may wait far longer than you need to.

Start by building evidence. Write down the work you’ve done, the outcomes you’ve created, the feedback you’ve received, and the challenges you’ve navigated. When self-doubt shows up, don’t only listen to the feeling. Look at the facts.

Then ask:

  • What would I do next if I trusted my capability?
  • Where am I waiting for permission that I may never receive?
  • What is one small step I can take this week to back myself?

Confidence is not about never doubting yourself. It’s about not letting doubt make all your decisions.

4. Strategic visibility

Hard work matters, but hard work alone is rarely enough. If people don’t understand your contribution, your aspirations or the value you create, you may be overlooked for opportunities you’re ready for.

Strategic visibility is not about being everywhere or constantly promoting yourself. It’s about making sure the right people understand the right things about your work.

This includes being clear about:

  • What you’re contributing
  • What impact your work is having
  • What you want to be known for
  • What kind of opportunities you’re ready for next

Many women feel uncomfortable with visibility because they associate it with bragging. But there’s a difference between performative self-promotion and clear, professional communication.

If you’ve led a project, solved a complex problem, improved an outcome, influenced a decision, or supported a major result, that information matters. It helps others understand your leadership and potential.

A practical place to start is your next one-to-one conversation. Instead of only updating your manager on tasks, include the impact of your work and what you’re learning about the level at which you want to contribute.

For example: “This project has given me the opportunity to work more strategically across stakeholders, and I’d like to build on that in the next quarter.”

That isn’t bragging; it’s career leadership, and it can make all the difference to what opportunities open up for you.

5. Boundaries that protect your capacity

You can’t build success on your own terms if your time and energy are constantly being consumed by everything and everyone else. Boundaries are essential because they protect the conditions you need to do meaningful work, think strategically, and stay well.

For many women, boundaries are difficult because they challenge long-standing patterns of being helpful, available, and accommodating. But without them, your priorities will always be vulnerable to other people’s urgency.

Start by looking at where your energy is going:

  • Are you saying yes to work that doesn’t align with your role or goals?
  • Are you attending meetings where you don’t need to be present?
  • Are you doing work that could be delegated, delayed, or redesigned?
  • Are you leaving your own development until last?

Boundaries don’t need to be dramatic. They might look like blocking time for strategic work, asking for clearer priorities, declining a meeting that isn’t necessary, or being more honest about capacity. Success on your own terms requires enough space to actually make choices.

6. Support and accountability

No woman should have to build her career alone. Yet many women try to do exactly that. They carry the pressure privately, try to figure out the next step alone, and assume they should already know how to navigate confidence, visibility, negotiation, leadership, and change.

Support changes what’s possible.

That support might come from a mentor, sponsor, peer network, coach, leadership program, or trusted community. You need people and structures that help you think clearly, stay accountable, and keep moving.

Career success on your own terms is not only an individual project. It’s supported by the conversations, relationships, and environments you surround yourself with.

If you’re serious about the next stage of your career, ask:

  • Who knows what I want next?
  • Who is helping me think bigger?
  • Who can support, challenge, or advocate for me?
  • What structure would help me follow through?

Sometimes the most powerful step is allowing yourself to be supported.

A final thought

Career success on your own terms is not about rejecting ambition. It’s about refining it.

It’s about building a career that reflects your values, uses your strengths, supports your well-being and gives you room to grow in a way that feels meaningful.

You don’t have to keep following a version of success that leaves you exhausted, unseen, or disconnected from yourself. You can define success differently. You can lead differently. You can make decisions that honor both your career and your life.

item.title: Backlash Is Proof of Progress
item.description:
Cross-Cultural Psychology

Backlash Is Proof of Progress

Backlash is often an essential part of culture change.

Posted July 8, 2026

Key points
  • While “greenlash” is clouding climate adaptation efforts, it’s not the end of the story.
  • Backlash and backsliding are normal, even expected, parts of change.
  • Savvy changemakers anticipate backlash and devise strategies to predict, address, or even counter it.
Source: Mark König / Unsplash

Summer is here—along with alarming reminders that something’s amiss with the climate. From record-breaking heatwaves to increased wildfire risk to violent storms, summer now feels like a season to survive rather than savor. "Coolcations" are now a thing: Instead of sweating through Southern Europe, travelers are chasing cooler temperatures in places like Scandinavia and Alaska.

It's no surprise that people feel pessimistic about the climate and our ability to avert the worst consequences. Climate- or eco-anxiety is on the rise, especially among young people. At the same time, greenlash—the social and political backlash against climate policy and adaptation efforts—is sweeping the U.S. and Europe, driven by populism and the culture wars. Even before the current backlash, making progress on climate issues has been hard for a host of reasons, ranging from designing effective policy and economic incentives to inconsistent governmental and organizational commitment to motivating collective and individual action. It can feel pretty hopeless that we’re in a downswing, yet again.

Greenlash, however, doesn’t have to be a reason for despair. When it comes to change, we don’t have to view backlash as a failure; we can instead see it as a sign of progress.

Culture change isn’t linear

Research in psychology and across the social sciences shows that backlash and backsliding are normal, even expected, parts of societal, organizational, and behavioral transformation. Shaking up the status quo often spurs challenge, resistance, and setbacks.

Ideally, we can do more to anticipate likely forms of backlash before they occur. It’s natural during the change processes to bump up against norms, narratives, and attitudes that cause friction or opposition. This is particularly true when change is viewed over a longer, more holistic time horizon—it’s back-and-forth, up-and-down, ever-shifting, not linear. This is why the next principle in the intentional culture change framework is #6: Culture change is not a linear path.

Take, for example, climate adaptation—one of the biggest, thorniest problems humanity faces. It will require large-scale cultural change, shifting how we live and what we do across the Culture Cycle (ideas, institutions, interactions, and individuals). So rather than accepting backlash as a sign of failure, we can instead learn to perceive it as a signal that meaningful change is underway.

Backlash is much like the recoil of a gun: You can brace for it or design the gun to reduce it, but you can’t fire the gun without it. Likewise, when we work to shift culture with intention, we need to brace for impact—the change process isn’t simply going to be smooth sailing. And it likely won’t progress as expected or along a straight path. It’s important to anticipate and prepare for the long and winding road that true transformation often takes.

The Culture Cycle
Source: MarYam Hamedani

Buckle your seatbelt

Being prepared for backlash doesn’t mean passive anticipation. Whatever our role—as a climate changemaker or concerned individual—we can do more to expect the kinds of greenlash climate adaptation is likely to encounter, and devise strategies to defuse or even counter them. Using Principle #5, we can anticipate who may feel threatened by change and why, and strategize to bring more stakeholders on board, even detractors. This is a place where the Culture Cycle comes in handy. It can help us discover and map sources of conflicts and key tension points in the current culture, think through which conflicts or tensions change could rock or inflame, and suggest mitigation strategies. For instance, where might diverse stakeholders share goals, values, and interests? Can we cast a bigger tent and help more people feel aligned with the change?

Let’s look at two common sources of greenlash at different points in the Culture Cycle. At the institutions level, U.S. companies have pulled back from ESG (ethics, society, and governance) initiatives in the current political climate, moving away from pro-environment efforts. Despite this corporate backlash, green technologies like solar energy are outstripping even the most optimistic predictions, driven by low costs and high demand. This incongruity shows that while companies may be shifting their strategies and rhetoric due to the political landscape, business and economic conditions continue to drive renewable energy growth. Change is happening—but it may be more aligned with today’s politics for companies to highlight economic benefits rather than ethical ones.

Another familiar source of greenlash exists at the individuals level, because many people feel like their individual actions don’t matter when it comes to the climate. While research shows that some actions do have more impact than others (voting compared to recycling), individuals can and do make a difference. So if people can learn more about which individual actions matter most, and maybe even feel good about doing them, they’ll commit to those actions—and bring others along, too. This research and other studies like it show that one way to defuse individual backlash is with information and empowerment.

Remember: Culture change is dynamic and iterative; it’s ongoing work that’s never really done. At some point, changemakers will encounter rough waters and setbacks. But we can do more to be ready and nimble—and recognize backlash as proof of progress.

Intentional Culture Change: 7 Key Principles
Source: MarYam Hamedani
